etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English punischen, from Anglo-Norman, Old French puniss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of punir, from Latin puniō (“I inflict punishment upon”), from poena (“punishment, penalty”); see pain. Displaced Old English wītnian and (mostly, in this sense) wrecan.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to suffer for crime or misconduct, to administer disciplinary action.

quote.citation: 1818, William Cobbett, The Parliamentary History of England, from the Earliest Period to the Year 1803, page 255:
quote.text: It was not from the want of proper laws that dangerous principles had been disseminated, and had assumed a threatening aspect, but because those laws had not been employed by the executive power to remedy the evil, and to punish the offenders.

quote.citation: 2007, Matthew Weait, Intimacy and Responsibility: The Criminalisation of HIV Transmission, Routledge, →ISBN, page 80:
quote.text: The law needs to punish this behaviour as a deterrent to others.

quote.citation: 2017, Joyce Carol Oates, Double Delight, Open Road Media, →ISBN:
quote.text: His mother had punished him when he'd deserved it. She'd loved him, he was “all she had,” but she'd punished him, too.

definitions.definition: (transitive, figuratively) To treat harshly and unfairly.

quote.citation: 1994, Valerie Polakow, Lives on the Edge: Single Mothers and Their Children in the Other America, University of Chicago Press, →ISBN, page 68:
quote.text: But each effort that Anna makes —and she has attempted many— meets with obstacles from a welfare bureaucracy that punishes single mothers for initiative and partial economic self-sufficiency.

quote.citation: 2008, Seth Benardete, The Bow and the Lyre: A Platonic Reading of the Odyssey, Rowman & Littlefield Publishers, →ISBN, page 5:
quote.text: Homer, moreover, gives the impression that the Sun punished Odysseus's men; but we are later told that the Sun cannot punish individual men  […]

quote.citation: 2009, Gordon Wright, Learning to Ride, Hunt, and Show, Skyhorse Publishing Inc., →ISBN, page 44:
quote.text: The rider who comes back on his horse in mid-air over a fence is punishing his horse severely.

definitions.definition: (transitive, colloquial) To handle or beat severely; to maul.
(transitive, colloquial) To consume a large quantity of.

quote.citation: 1970, Doc Greene, The Memory Collector, page 49:
quote.text: A few moments later, we were all sitting around the veranda of the hunters' dining hall, punishing the gin, as usual.
